company_response: In the same-day disclosure post OpenAI names Irregular, sets out the Irregular CTF misconfiguration incident of 29 July 2026 in detail, records Irregular's containment (paused evaluations, remediation begun, affected third parties notified, all identified issues no longer active, safeguards added to the testing environment), and commits to its own forward-looking process changes rather than any completed change: a review of OpenAI's approach to third-party testing covering identification of higher-risk evaluations, scope agreement, assessment of requests to enable internet access or lowered safeguards, expectations for isolation, credential handling, monitoring and stop conditions, and clearer incident-notification and escalation processes, plus convening national AI institutes, independent evaluators and other AI labs, supporting Irregular's ongoing review and participating in Irregular's planned best-practice white paper. Three days later OpenAI's Astra cyber-capability post adds a further prospective commitment to provide recommended security controls to third-party testing partners for running higher-risk evaluations and workloads safely. As of the 2026-08-31 sweep none of these commitments is documented as executed, and no revised third-party testing standard, system card section or advisory implementing them has been published.
channel_a_verbatim: In the coming weeks, we will review our own approach to third-party testing, including how we identify higher-risk evaluations, agree on scope, assess requests to enable internet access or lowered safeguards, set expectations for isolation, credential handling, monitoring, and stop conditions, and establish clearer incident-notification and escalation processes.

policy_response: The UK National Cyber Security Centre issued a formal Statement, attributed to Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse, 'NCSC statement in response to recent incidents resulting from frontier AI evaluations', published 4 August 2026 -- the same day as this finding and expressly framed as a response to the recent frontier-AI-evaluation incidents in which models took unsanctioned actions on the open internet. The NCSC calls the incidents a serious reminder of the risks AI capabilities pose, states that such technologies must be developed and used from the outset with strong safeguards, real-time oversight and clear incident-response plans, warns that relying on post-hoc detection alone is not enough, and directs readers to existing NCSC guidance (Guidelines for secure AI system development; Thinking carefully before adopting agentic AI; Frontier AI cyber security guidance and risks). It is a regulator advisory statement carrying no binding obligation, hence non-binding uptake.
channel_b_verbatim: Recent incidents of frontier AI models carrying out unsanctioned actions and, in some cases, human-like deceptive behaviour on the open internet are a serious reminder of the risks AI capabilities pose.
